topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Function calls and dynamic allocation have costs and limits that are not visible in a class diagram. A stack frame is an implementation mechanism for an active call; an allocator manages reusable storage and its own metadata. We will observe a bounded recursive call chain and count requests through a polymorphic memory resource, carefully distinguishing requested bytes from allocator overhead and operating-system memory usage.

blocks.text: This chapter connects call-stack reasoning with scoped heap accounting. Both require precise boundaries. Neither should be mistaken for a complete description of every byte used by the process.

topics.title: 4.1.1 Storing Parameters and Local Variables
topics.summary: A calling convention specifies how a compiled function receives arguments, returns results, and preserves required machine state. Some arguments may be passed in registers and others in memory. A function can reserve stack space for locals or spills, but optimization may eliminate, combine, or relocate those objects.

blocks.text: A function invocation needs a way to receive arguments, preserve required state, and resume its caller. A calling convention specifies parts of that arrangement for a particular ABI. Arguments may travel in registers, memory, or a combination. A compiler can also inline a function so that no separate machine-level call remains. The source signature describes the language interface, not an instruction-by-instruction transfer plan.

blocks.text: Within an active invocation, automatic objects have lifetimes governed by their declarations and control flow. A compiler may place some in a stack frame, reuse storage for objects whose lifetimes do not overlap, or keep values elsewhere. Taking an address can affect what storage must be materialized, but even then the implementation must be interpreted through the language’s observable behavior rather than a universal source-to-stack formula.

blocks.text: Consider a function with a local buffer and a helper that borrows it. The borrow is safe only while the object exists and the access is otherwise valid. Calling the helper synchronously is different from enqueueing a callback that retains the pointer after the function returns. The latter changes the lifetime requirement even if the helper’s parameter type stays identical. A raw pointer does not communicate that difference by itself.

blocks.text: Debuggers show frames using available unwind information and debug metadata. Optimized code can make source variables unavailable, combine instructions from several source lines, or eliminate a frame through inlining. These effects complicate inspection without changing the source contract. For a first investigation, use a debug build and a small call chain; then compare an optimized build while keeping the explanation modest.

blocks.text: In the worked function, each invocation receives a bounded nonnegative depth and contributes that value to a recursive sum. Draw the active calls for depth four before examining the debugger: four waits for three, three for two, and so on until zero returns. This trace describes logical invocations. Whether the compiler retains exactly those machine frames is a separate observation. A public function accepting arbitrary depth would require validation and a resource bound; the private teaching call does not establish a general recursion API.

topics.title: 4.1.2 Understanding Return Addresses
topics.summary: The execution mechanism must preserve enough information to continue after a call, often including a return address and saved state according to the architecture. That state is not a portable C++ object that application code should modify. Corrupting it through an out-of-bounds write is undefined behavior and a serious security defect.

blocks.text: A backtrace reconstructs call history using available unwind metadata, frame conventions, and debug information. Optimizations, omitted frames, corrupted memory, or missing symbols can limit the result. Treat a trace as evidence with those limitations, and preserve the matching binary and symbols when diagnosing a failure.

blocks.text: A return address is part of the machine’s mechanism for resuming execution after a call. Its storage and manipulation are ABI- and architecture-specific. Ordinary C++ does not provide a portable entitlement to walk arbitrary stack memory until something resembles a code address. Use a debugger’s stack trace or supported unwind facilities rather than inventing pointer arithmetic across implementation state.
rich: A return address is part of the machine’s mechanism for resuming execution after a call. Its storage and manipulation are ABI- and architecture-specific. Ordinary C++ does not provide a portable entitlement to walk arbitrary stack memory until something resembles a code address. Use a debugger’s stack trace or supported unwind facilities rather than inventing pointer arithmetic across implementation state.

blocks.text: Destruction during normal return is governed by C++ object lifetime. Exception propagation adds another path: successfully constructed automatic objects in exited scopes are destroyed while the exception moves toward a handler. This is the mechanism RAII relies on. A native resource wrapper should therefore release its owned handle during unwinding without throwing a second exception from its destructor. The presence of a return address does not itself perform that cleanup; language and runtime machinery cooperate.

blocks.text: Tail-call optimization illustrates the gap between logical calls and retained frames. An implementation may replace an eligible final call with a transfer that reuses the caller’s execution storage. The source can still be understood as a call, while the debugger may not display every apparent invocation. Do not base a correctness argument on a particular stack-trace shape. In particular, absence of a frame is not evidence that the source function was never involved.

blocks.text: Security-sensitive diagnosis also needs boundaries. A corrupt return path can be a symptom of memory damage, but this book’s lab does not overwrite stack state or demonstrate control-flow exploitation. The useful engineering exercise is to prevent the preceding invalid write, retain diagnostic builds, and identify the first violation. A crash at return often occurs after the original defect, so the last visible frame is not automatically the root cause.

blocks.text: For a reproducible report, retain the exact executable and matching debug information. A stack trace interpreted with symbols from a different build can assign convincing but wrong source locations. Source revision, optimization flags, architecture, and binary identity belong together. Treat the trace as evidence from that artifact, then connect it back to the ownership, bounds, and lifetime contracts that should have prevented the invalid state.

topics.title: 4.2.1 Understanding Allocator Metadata
topics.summary: An allocator tracks free and in-use regions using implementation-specific metadata. A request for N bytes may cause additional bookkeeping, alignment padding, or a larger reserved block. Different allocation sizes may use different internal paths. The C++ allocation interface does not promise that requested bytes equal total process memory cost.

blocks.text: A request for a block of storage is not necessarily a request for one equally sized physical-memory allocation. A general-purpose allocator can divide arenas, round sizes, retain freed blocks, and maintain metadata. Its upstream interaction with the operating system can occur less frequently than application-level allocation. That layering explains why counting new expressions, allocator calls, and system calls produces different totals.

blocks.text: The chapter’s CountingResource intercepts requests through one polymorphic memory resource. It forwards allocation to an upstream resource, then records the requested byte count and alignment-related operation. The counter describes successful requests it sees. It does not intercept every allocation in the process, and it does not know the upstream allocator’s internal bookkeeping or page residency. Those limitations are not defects; they define the instrument.

A production accounting facility would also need policies for counter overflow, concurrency, and misuse of the deallocation contract.

blocks.text: Resource lifetime is an ownership dependency. A pmr::vector using a borrowed memory resource must not outlive that resource. Declaring the resource before the vector’s scope makes the dependency visible: the vector destroys its elements and releases storage before the resource is destroyed. A pointer to a resource is not shared ownership. Moving a container or storing it elsewhere can invalidate an otherwise-correct local lifetime argument. (MEMORY)

blocks.text: Nested allocation deserves separate attention. A container whose elements are ordinary std::string objects does not automatically route every character allocation through the outer container’s PMR resource. Choose allocator-aware element types and understand propagation when the accounting contract requires nested allocations to be included. The integer-vector example avoids that extra layer so the observed counts can be explained without pretending they cover a more complex object graph.

topics.summary: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside allocated blocks due to rounding or alignment; external fragmentation is free space split into pieces that may not satisfy a desired larger request under an allocator’s policy. blocks.text: A high resident set after freeing objects does not alone identify fragmentation. The allocator may cache reusable memory, the operating system may retain pages, and unrelated allocations may still be live. Build a repeatable workload and use suitable allocator or heap-profiler evidence before changing memory management. A custom allocator can improve one pattern while making another worse.

blocks.text: Fragmentation describes ways storage can be available yet inconveniently organized or partly unused. Internal fragmentation concerns space inside allocated units that the workload cannot use directly, such as size rounding. External fragmentation concerns free space divided into pieces that may not satisfy a larger request under an allocator’s constraints. These are useful concepts, but a process-level memory chart does not directly separate them.
rich: Fragmentation describes ways storage can be available yet inconveniently organized or partly unused. External fragmentation concerns free space divided into pieces that may not satisfy a larger request under an allocator’s constraints. blocks.text: Container capacity is another form of retained space, not necessarily allocator fragmentation. A vector can contain ten elements while reserving room for many more. That capacity may be an intentional tradeoff to avoid future reallocations. Calling it a leak confuses retained ownership with lost ownership. Conversely, keeping excessive capacity across thousands of long-lived objects can violate a memory budget even though the implementation is memory-safe.

blocks.text: Compare three quantities in the worked example: current element count, allocated capacity expressed in element bytes, and peak requested bytes observed by the resource. They can differ without contradiction. During growth, a container may temporarily hold old and new storage while transferring elements; the peak can exceed the final allocation. Reserving once before a known bounded workload changes that allocation history, but it does not prove lower total resident memory for the entire application.

blocks.text: Do not solve every fragmentation concern with a custom pool. Specialized allocation adds lifetime, alignment, exhaustion, and observability obligations. A pool can be appropriate for a measured workload with predictable object sizes and phases, but it can also retain large blocks indefinitely or hide stale references after reuse. Chapter 10 develops bounded arenas and generation-checked handles. Here the priority is measurement discipline: identify the allocation boundary and the workload before deciding that the default allocator is the bottleneck.

topics.title: Failure clinic — A dangling allocator outlives its stack frame
topics.summary: A helper constructs a local memory resource and returns a container that still refers to it. The container’s element values look correct on return, but later allocation or destruction accesses a dead resource. The failure is a lifetime defect, not a mysterious allocator bug. Return an object that owns the resource appropriately, accept a caller-owned resource with a clear lifetime contract, or use a container whose allocator does not borrow local state.

Compare an optimized build and describe missing or transformed information without treating it as a semantic failure. Keep the exact executable identities with both observations.

Finally, draw the lifetime dependency for a PMR container and its resource. Mark destruction order explicitly. Propose a safe interface for a caller that wants the container to survive a helper function. The answer must identify an owner, not simply move the dangling resource pointer into a different variable.

Review reasoning. Does a successful deallocation imply an immediate resident-memory decrease? No. Are capacity and size the same? No. Does a PMR resource automatically observe every nested allocation? Only when the relevant allocator-aware types and propagation actually route those requests through it. Does a source function require a distinct retained frame after optimization? Not universally.

Completion criterion. Supply the two equal results, the distinct allocation histories, and an explicit resource-lifetime diagram. A sound conclusion names the measured improvement precisely instead of declaring one allocation strategy universally superior.
